ingredients: Purpose-made flood barriers or boards for doorways, sized and trial-fitted in advance; improvised sandbags are far less effective and need roughly twenty-five to thirty bags for a single doorway
Non-return valves fitted to toilet, sink and floor-drain connections, which prevent sewage backing up through fixtures when the sewer surcharges
Airbrick covers or plugs matched to the openings on your building
Heavy plastic sheeting and waterproof tape for sealing low openings and covering stored goods
A submersible pump with a hose long enough to discharge well away from the building, plus an independent power source if you rely on it
A battery or wind-up radio, torches with spare batteries, and a power bank, since mains power commonly fails
Waterproof storage for documents, medication, keys, cash and chargers, kept above the likely water level
Rubber boots and heavy waterproof gloves; never wade in open footwear
A first aid kit including plenty of waterproof dressings, and antiseptic, because floodwater infects minor wounds readily
Bottled drinking water for at least three days, because supply may be interrupted or contaminated

sections.heading: What To Do While the Water Is Rising
sections.body:
Once flooding is underway, the decisions that matter are few and they must be made quickly. The governing principle throughout is that property can be replaced and people cannot, so no step below is worth taking if it delays leaving when leaving is the right call. The single most important rule in all flood safety is to stay out of moving water and never to drive into it.

The order below is roughly the order of priority under time pressure. If the water is already at the door, skip directly to getting people upward and out; the protective measures are for the window between the warning and the water, which in pluvial flooding may be only twenty or thirty minutes.
steps: Decide immediately whether to stay or leave, and if there is any doubt, leave early while the roads are still passable on foot. Leaving late, through rising water, is far more dangerous than leaving early for nothing.

Move upward, not downward. Get out of basements and ground-floor flats at the first sign of water entering, before doors become impossible to open. Do not shelter in a cellar or an underground car park.

Turn off electricity at the consumer unit, and gas at the meter, but only if the isolation point is dry and you can reach it without standing in water. If it is already submerged, leave it alone and call the utility.
Move a vehicle to higher ground now, while the road is clear, or accept that it will be lost. Do not go back for it once water is running.

Lift what you can above the expected level: electrical items, documents, photographs, medicines, food. Put furniture legs on blocks. Take small valuables upstairs rather than trying to move heavy things.
Fit door barriers and airbrick covers, and close and weight down toilet lids if you have no non-return valves, since sewage backing up is a common entry route.
Fill a bath and containers with clean water before the supply is affected, and charge phones and power banks while mains power lasts.
If water enters despite this, stop defending the building and move to the highest safe floor with your emergency supplies, phone, warm clothing and something bright or reflective to signal with.
Call the emergency number if anyone is trapped, in the water, or in a vehicle, and give the exact address and the number of people. Do not wait to see if it improves.

If you are swept off your feet, get onto your back with feet downstream and pointed up to fend off obstacles, keep your head up, and swim across the flow toward the edge rather than fighting against it.
Never enter a culvert, drain, ditch or channel to retrieve anything or anyone; the intake force pins a body against the grating and rescuers have died this way.

sections.heading: Vehicles and Floodwater: The Decision That Kills Most People
sections.body:
Across many countries and many decades, the same statistic recurs with depressing consistency: roughly half to three-quarters of flood fatalities involve vehicles. The pattern is not random ignorance. It reflects a specific and very human misjudgement — a driver looks at water across a road, sees a surface rather than a depth, compares it with previous crossings that were fine, and drives on. The water is nearly always deeper than it looks, because the road dips where the water collects, and moving water hides the fact that the surface beneath may have been washed away entirely.

The engineering is not in the driver's favour. Buoyancy acts on the whole submerged volume of the vehicle, and a car is mostly air. Around 15 centimetres of moving water can cause loss of control; at roughly 30 centimetres many cars begin to lift and lose traction; by 60 centimetres the great majority of passenger cars float. Once floating, the vehicle has no steering, no braking and no grip, and a current of even one metre per second exerts a sideways force sufficient to move it. Four-wheel drive and greater weight help only marginally; larger vehicles float at greater depths but they float. A vehicle carried off the road frequently ends up in a ditch, inverted, or in water deep enough to submerge it entirely.

The escape problem is severe. Modern cars have electric windows that fail within seconds to minutes of the electrical system flooding, and doors that cannot be opened against a water level difference of more than a few tens of centimetres. Laminated side glass, increasingly common, cannot be broken with a spring-loaded punch designed for tempered glass. If a vehicle is entering water, the correct response is to release seatbelts, open a window immediately while it still works, and get out through the window before the car is committed; the widely repeated advice to wait for the car to fill so pressures equalise is a last resort that assumes you have failed at everything earlier.

The rule that has been promoted for decades in the United States and elsewhere is deliberately simple because simple rules survive panic: turn around, don't drown. Never drive through water of unknown depth. Never drive around a barrier closing a flooded road; the barrier is there because the road may no longer exist beneath the water. Never assume a route you use daily is safe, since scour can remove a carriageway or undermine a bridge approach in a single event.

If a vehicle stalls in rising water, abandon it immediately and move to higher ground on foot if the water is shallow and slow enough to walk in, or climb onto the roof and call for help if it is not. A car is replaceable and takes seconds to leave. People die in cars because they spend those seconds deciding.

sections.heading: After the Water Goes Down: Contamination, Drying and Health
sections.body:
The recovery phase causes far more illness and injury than the flood itself, and it is where most avoidable harm occurs, largely because the sense of danger has passed while the actual hazards have not.

Assume floodwater is contaminated. In a combined sewer city it is a sewage dilution, and even in separate systems it carries road runoff, animal faeces, agricultural residue and whatever came out of flooded fuel tanks, garages and workshops. The pathogens of concern include Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, Giardia, hepatitis A and, in some regions, leptospirosis, which is transmitted through rat urine and enters through broken skin or mucous membranes and can be fatal. Tetanus risk is elevated by any wound in contaminated water. Practical implications: wear waterproof gloves and boots, cover every cut with a waterproof dressing before entering, wash hands thoroughly before eating or smoking, and seek medical attention for any wound sustained in floodwater or for fever, jaundice or severe muscle pain in the following two weeks.

Do not drink or cook with tap water until the supplier confirms it is safe, since mains can be contaminated by infiltration or by loss of pressure. Discard all food that has contacted floodwater, including tinned goods with damaged seams and anything in a permeable package. Refrigerated food is unsafe after roughly four hours without power; frozen food that still contains ice crystals and is at or below four degrees Celsius may be refrozen, but anything warmer should be thrown out.

Electrical safety remains the acute danger. Do not restore power until the installation has been inspected by a competent person, and do not use appliances that have been submerged, however dry they now appear. Never run a petrol generator, pressure washer, or fuel-burning heater or pump inside a building, garage or basement: carbon monoxide from generators kills people during flood recovery every year, and the gas is odourless and accumulates faster than intuition allows.

Drying determines whether the building recovers. Standing water should be removed, then the structure dried steadily rather than aggressively, since drying masonry too fast causes cracking. Plaster and plasterboard commonly wick water well above the visible line and generally need cutting back to at least 30 to 50 centimetres above it. Insulation in cavities and floors retains water and usually must be replaced. Full drying of masonry takes weeks to months, and a rough working figure of one month per 25 millimetres of wall thickness is often quoted. Mould establishes within 24 to 48 hours on damp organic material, so ventilation and dehumidification should start immediately, and anyone with asthma or immune compromise should stay away from heavy mould growth.

Finally, photograph and document everything before removing it, for insurance, and keep receipts. And recognise the mental health dimension: flood recovery is prolonged, exhausting and demoralising, and psychological effects commonly outlast the physical damage.

sections.heading: Clearing and Maintaining Drains Safely
sections.body:
A surprising amount of urban flooding is preventable by unglamorous maintenance, and much of it is within the reach of ordinary residents. The caveat is that some of it is genuinely dangerous and should not be attempted.

The safe and useful work is at the surface. Clearing leaves, litter and silt off a gully grate before and during the wet season restores most of its capacity, and this single action prevents a large share of minor street flooding. Autumn leaf fall and the first heavy rains of the season are the critical period. A stiff brush, a rake and a shovel are sufficient; the debris should be bagged and disposed of rather than swept into the next gully downstream. Clearing gutters and downpipes on the building, and checking that the downpipe actually discharges into a drain rather than onto the ground beside the wall, is equally worthwhile. Silt traps and channel gratings around driveways need the same attention.

What should not be attempted without training and equipment is anything involving entry. A drainage chamber, manhole or culvert is a confined space, and confined spaces kill people with grim regularity, usually in pairs or threes as would-be rescuers follow the first casualty in. The hazards are hydrogen sulphide, which is produced by decomposing sewage, smells of rotten eggs at low concentrations and then paralyses the sense of smell so that rising concentrations are undetectable; methane, which displaces oxygen and is explosive; carbon dioxide accumulation and simple oxygen deficiency; and drowning from sudden flow. Never lift a manhole cover and climb in, never send anyone in on a rope without proper gas monitoring, rescue equipment and trained standby personnel, and never enter a culvert.

Equally, never remove a manhole cover during flooding to help the water drain. This creates a hidden vertical shaft under moving opaque water, and it is a well-documented way that both residents and responders have drowned. If a cover has already been displaced by pressure, mark the location conspicuously with a barrier, a cone, a chair, anything visible, and warn others.

Blockages inside a private drain run can often be cleared with drain rods worked from an accessible chamber, though pushing a blockage further into a shared sewer merely relocates the problem. Persistent blockage, collapse, or root intrusion needs a professional with a jetting unit and a camera survey.

Report what you cannot fix. Municipal drainage authorities generally maintain gullies on a cycle that is longer than ideal, and they rely substantially on reports to prioritise. A gully that has not drained for weeks, a manhole that surcharges in every storm, a blocked culvert screen or a watercourse choked with fly-tipped material are all worth reporting specifically, with a location and a photograph, before the season rather than during the storm.

sections.heading: Designing Flooding Out: Sustainable Drainage and Sponge Cities
sections.body:
The engineering response to urban flooding has shifted substantially over the past half-century, away from the assumption that water should be captured and removed as fast as possible and toward the recognition that speed of removal is itself part of the problem. Conveying runoff downstream quickly simply relocates the peak, and where thousands of small developments each do so, the cumulative effect is to make downstream flooding worse. The modern approach — variously called sustainable drainage systems or SuDS in Britain, low impact development in North America, water sensitive urban design in Australia, and the sponge city concept in China — attempts instead to restore some of the storage and delay that development removed.

The techniques form a hierarchy. At source, permeable paving allows water to infiltrate through the surface into a granular sub-base that stores it temporarily; green roofs retain the first several millimetres of rainfall in a growing medium and release the rest slowly; rain gardens and bioretention areas are shallow planted depressions that take roof and road runoff, hold it briefly and let it soak away; water butts and rainwater harvesting capture a modest volume for reuse. Downstream, swales are vegetated channels that convey water slowly and allow infiltration along the way, and detention basins and retention ponds store peak flows and release them at a controlled rate through a restricted outlet. The design target is typically to limit discharge to the greenfield runoff rate — the flow the site would have produced before development.

The co-benefits are substantial and are often what actually gets these schemes funded: vegetated systems remove pollutants from road runoff, provide habitat and shade, reduce the urban heat island effect, and are generally more pleasant than a concrete channel. Their limitations are equally real. Infiltration systems do not work on clay soils or where the water table is high; they can be rendered useless by silt if not maintained; permeable paving clogs over time and needs periodic vacuum sweeping; and none of them can absorb a genuinely extreme storm. They shave the peak of frequent events very effectively and matter much less in the rarest ones.

Alongside these sits an older and simpler idea now returning to favour: give water somewhere to go. Daylighting culverted streams, restoring floodplains, designating parks and sports pitches as controlled flood storage, and designing streets deliberately as temporary channels toward safe outlets all accept that in an extreme event water will move across the surface, and try to determine where. Rotterdam's water squares, which function as public plazas most of the time and as storage basins in storms, and Tokyo's enormous underground discharge channel, are two ends of the same philosophical spectrum. The most important measure of all remains land use planning: not building in the places that flood.

sections.heading: Limits, Failure Modes and When It Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Several honest limitations should temper any confidence about urban flood safety, and knowing them changes how you behave.

The first is that no drainage system is designed for the worst case, and this is a deliberate economic decision rather than negligence. Every city will experience storms beyond its design standard. The correct mental model is not "the drains will cope" but "the drains will cope until they do not, and I should know what happens then." Where a city has planned major flow routes, the excess travels along designated streets to open ground. Where it has not, it goes wherever the topography sends it, which is frequently through buildings.

The second is that flood maps are incomplete in a specific and dangerous way. Most published maps show river and coastal flood zones well, because those are computed from channel hydraulics and gauge records. Surface water flooding is far less consistently mapped, is much harder to model, and can occur anywhere — including on ground shown as entirely outside any flood zone. A property outside the mapped floodplain is not a property that cannot flood, and in many cities pluvial flooding affects more homes than fluvial does.

The third is non-stationarity. Flood frequency statistics assume the past is a guide to the future, and warming has undermined that assumption in a specific way: warmer air holds more moisture, at roughly seven per cent more per degree Celsius by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation, and observed short-duration rainfall extremes have in many regions intensified at that rate or somewhat faster. Combined with continuing urbanisation, this means the design storm used to size an existing network may already be exceeded more often than its stated return period implies. Treat old return-period labels as optimistic.

The fourth is that infrastructure fails in correlated ways. Severe storms cut power, and power loss stops pumps, traffic signals, communications and water treatment simultaneously. Emergency services are saturated during widespread events, and response times that are minutes on an ordinary day become hours. Plan on the assumption that no one is coming quickly.

When things go wrong, the priorities compress to a short list. Get above the water and stay there rather than attempting to move through it. Do not enter, drive into, or wade through moving water of unknown depth for any reason, including to reach a vehicle, a pet or possessions. Do not enter basements or underground spaces once water is entering. Assume the water is contaminated and electrically live. Signal your position and wait; a bright cloth at a window, a torch and a charged phone are more useful than heroics. Help neighbours who cannot self-evacuate — the elderly, the disabled, families with small children — early rather than late, since evacuation becomes rapidly harder as depth increases. And afterwards, treat the recovery hazards with the same seriousness as the flood, because carbon monoxide, electricity and infection cause more casualties than the water did.

guides.safetyNote: Never drive or walk into floodwater of unknown depth: about 30 cm can float a car and 0.5 m of moving water can knock down an adult. Treat all floodwater as sewage-contaminated and potentially electrically live, never enter a drain, culvert or confined chamber, and never run a generator or fuel-burning pump indoors.

guides.title: Coastal Storm Surge Mechanics
guides.summary: How storms push seawater onto land: the physics of wind stress, pressure and waves, why shallow shelves and funnelling bays amplify surge, how tides, rivers and sea-level rise compound it, and how surge is forecast, mapped, defended against and survived.

sections.heading: What Storm Surge Is, and Why It Is the Thing That Kills
sections.body:
Storm surge is the abnormal rise of seawater above the level the tide alone would have produced, generated by a storm's winds and low pressure pushing the ocean against a coast. It is not a wave in the ordinary sense, and this is the single most important thing to understand about it. A wave rises and falls in seconds. A surge is a bodily rise of the whole sea surface that arrives over minutes to hours and stays for hours, carrying breaking waves on top of it. People who picture a wall of water are picturing the wrong thing; what usually happens is that the water simply keeps coming up, past the beach, past the road, past the door frame, and does not go down. 

Three terms are used precisely by forecasters and it is worth separating them because confusing them has cost lives. Storm surge is the rise above the predicted astronomical tide, measured in metres of anomaly. Storm tide is the total observed water level, that is surge plus tide, measured against a fixed vertical datum. Inundation, sometimes called water level above ground level, is how deep the water is where you are standing, which is storm tide minus the elevation of your ground. A three-metre surge arriving at low tide onto ground that stands four metres above the datum produces no flooding at all. The same surge at high spring tide onto ground one metre above datum puts water above head height in the street. Only the third number tells you whether to leave. 

The lethality is documented and stark. A review of United States tropical cyclone deaths from 1963 to 2012 by Edward Rappaport of the National Hurricane Center attributed roughly half of all direct fatalities to storm surge, with freshwater flooding from rainfall a distant second and wind a small minority. Historically the numbers are worse elsewhere. The 1970 Bhola cyclone drove water estimated at up to ten metres across the low deltaic islands of what is now Bangladesh and killed somewhere between 300,000 and 500,000 people, probably the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history. The 1900 Galveston hurricane put about four and a half metres of water over an island whose highest point was under three metres, killing at least six thousand and possibly twice that. The 1953 North Sea flood, driven not by a tropical cyclone but by a deep extratropical depression, killed about 1,836 people in the Netherlands, 307 in England and hundreds more at sea in a single night. 

In each case the wind was survivable and the water was not. This asymmetry is why coastal emergency managers repeat the phrase run from the water, hide from the wind.

sections.heading: The Three Forces That Raise the Water
sections.body:
Storm surge is produced by three distinct physical mechanisms acting together, and they contribute very unequally. Separating them explains almost every apparent anomaly in surge behaviour. 

The dominant mechanism is wind stress. A wind blowing across water exerts a horizontal drag on the surface, and that drag drives a current. Where the water is bounded by a coast, the current cannot continue and the water piles up instead, tilting the sea surface upward toward the shore until the pressure gradient from that tilt balances the wind's push. The surface stress is approximately the air density times a drag coefficient times the square of the wind speed, and because the wind speed is squared, doubling the wind roughly quadruples the stress. The resulting slope of the sea surface is the stress divided by water density, gravity, and crucially the water depth. That depth term in the denominator is the most consequential single fact in the whole subject: the shallower the water, the steeper the wind can tilt it. 

A worked example makes the scale concrete. Take a sustained wind of 40 metres per second, about 145 kilometres per hour, a strong category two hurricane. Air density is about 1.2 kilograms per cubic metre and the drag coefficient over rough seas is roughly 0.0025, giving a surface stress near 4.8 pascals. Over a shelf 20 metres deep, the sea surface slope is that stress divided by water density times gravity times depth, about 4.8 divided by 200,000, or 2.4 hundred-thousandths. Multiply by a shelf 100 kilometres wide and you get about 2.4 metres of wind-driven setup at the coast. Run the same calculation over a shelf 200 metres deep and you get about 0.24 metres. Same storm, ten times the surge, purely because of what lies underwater. 

The second mechanism is the inverse barometer effect. A storm's low central pressure lifts the sea beneath it, because less air is pressing down there than on the surrounding ocean. The relationship is close to one centimetre of sea-level rise for each hectopascal of pressure deficit. A hurricane with a central pressure of 950 hectopascals sitting in an ambient field of 1013 therefore lifts the ocean beneath it by about 63 centimetres. This sounds substantial and is usually a modest fraction of the total; in a major surge event it contributes perhaps ten to twenty per cent. 

The third mechanism is wave-induced. Breaking waves transfer momentum shoreward, raising the mean water level inside the surf zone in an effect called wave setup, typically on the order of five to twenty per cent of the offshore significant wave height. On steep coasts and coral reef fronts, where the shelf is too narrow for much wind setup, wave setup and wave runup can dominate entirely.

sections.heading: Why Bathymetry Decides Almost Everything
sections.body:
If you want to know how bad a surge can get at a given place, the first thing to look at is not the storm history but the depth chart. The inverse dependence of wind setup on water depth means that the width and shallowness of the continental shelf offshore is the single strongest predictor of surge potential, and it varies enormously around the world. 

The catastrophic locations share a profile: a broad, gently sloping shelf where water stays under fifty metres deep for a hundred kilometres or more, feeding into a coast that is itself low-lying. The northern Gulf of Mexico is the textbook case, and it produced the 8.5 metres of surge measured near Pass Christian, Mississippi during Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the highest ever recorded in the United States. The Bay of Bengal is worse still, combining an extremely shallow shelf with a converging coastline and a densely populated delta barely above sea level. The southern North Sea, the Yellow Sea and the northern coast of Australia are in the same category. 

At the other extreme are coasts where deep water comes almost to the shore. Volcanic islands with steep submarine flanks, much of the Pacific coast of the Americas, and the fringes of many Caribbean islands have shelves only a few kilometres wide. A hurricane of identical intensity that would drive six metres of water into a Gulf coast bay may produce well under a metre of surge on such a coast. That does not make those coasts safe; it changes the hazard's character. With deep water offshore, large ocean swell arrives at the beach unbroken, so wave runup, overtopping and impact loads become the dominant destructive process rather than a slow inundation. 

Two further bathymetric effects matter. The first is that shallow water also slows the surge, because the speed at which a long wave travels is the square root of gravity times depth. Over a shelf 50 metres deep that is about 22 metres per second, roughly 80 kilometres per hour. When a storm's forward speed happens to match that shallow-water wave speed, energy is fed continuously into the same disturbance for hours and the surge grows disproportionately, an amplification known as Proudman resonance. This is why forward speed and shelf depth interact rather than acting independently. 

The second is friction. A surge crossing a wide, very shallow shelf loses energy to bottom drag, and once it moves overland it loses much more, so inundation typically decreases with distance inland at a rate that depends strongly on land cover. Open water and bare ground offer little resistance; dense forest, mangrove and built-up terrain offer a great deal. The rule of thumb sometimes quoted, that surge decays by roughly a foot per mile inland, is a crude average that conceals a range from almost no decay across open marsh to rapid attenuation through vegetation.

sections.heading: Storm Size, Speed and Why Category Is the Wrong Number
sections.body:
The most persistent and dangerous public misconception about surge is that it scales with hurricane category. It does not, and the meteorological community formally acknowledged this in 2010 by stripping the storm surge ranges out of the Saffir-Simpson scale and renaming it the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. The scale now describes wind damage potential and nothing else, because the surge ranges it used to publish were misleading often enough to be a public safety problem. 

Four storm properties beyond peak wind speed control the surge, and the first is size. Wind stress acts over the entire area the storm covers, and the water it moves has to go somewhere, so a physically large storm mobilises far more water than a small intense one. The relevant measures are the radius of maximum winds and the radius of gale-force winds. Hurricane Ike in 2008 made landfall on the Texas coast with winds that rated only category two, but it was enormous, and it drove a surge of four to five metres, comparable to what a much stronger compact storm would have produced. Conversely, small intense hurricanes can produce surprisingly modest surge because the wind field simply does not have the fetch to shift enough water. 

The second property is forward speed, and its effect is genuinely two-sided. A slow-moving storm gives the ocean more time to respond, which raises the surge on gently sloping shelves where the water needs hours to pile up, and it prolongs the flooding across multiple tidal cycles. A fast-moving storm gives less time but delivers the water more abruptly and can outrun the drainage, which matters most on steep coasts and in estuaries. Where forward speed matches the shallow-water wave speed over the shelf, resonance amplifies the result well beyond what either factor alone would give. 

The third is the angle of approach. A storm that crosses the coast perpendicular concentrates its onshore winds over a short stretch of shoreline for a short time. A storm running parallel to the coast, or approaching obliquely, may drive onshore winds along hundreds of kilometres of coast for many hours, producing a broader if sometimes lower surge and flooding places far from the eventual landfall point. 

The fourth is duration and persistence, including the crucial detail that the wind must blow onshore. A storm may be intense and enormous and still produce very little surge at a given town if that town spends the whole event on the side where the wind blows offshore, which actually lowers the water below normal in a phenomenon called negative surge or blowout tide. Coastal residents have drowned after walking onto an exposed seabed during a blowout and being caught when the wind shifted and the water returned.

sections.heading: Rotation, the Right-Front Quadrant, and Where the Water Goes
sections.body:
Tropical cyclones rotate, and where a coastline sits relative to that rotation determines whether the storm pushes water toward it or drags water away. In the Northern Hemisphere, cyclones spin counter-clockwise, so the winds on the right side of the storm relative to its direction of travel blow in roughly the same direction the storm is moving, while the winds on the left blow against it. 

Two consequences follow. First, the right side experiences higher absolute wind speed, because the storm's forward motion adds to its rotational wind there and subtracts on the left; a storm with 150 kilometres per hour of rotational wind moving at 30 kilometres per hour has roughly 180 on the right and 120 on the left. Second, and more important for surge, the right-front quadrant is where onshore winds blow for the longest continuous period as the storm approaches. The combination makes the right-front quadrant the surge maximum in almost every Northern Hemisphere landfall. The practical rule is that the worst flooding occurs to the right of where the eye crosses the coast, typically within a zone tens of kilometres wide, while the coast to the left of landfall may see very little water or even negative surge. 

In the Southern Hemisphere everything mirrors: cyclones rotate clockwise and the surge maximum falls in the left-front quadrant, which matters for anyone reading guidance written for the other hemisphere. 

A subtler rotational effect is the Coriolis force acting on the wind-driven current itself. Water set in motion by wind does not travel directly downwind; it is deflected, to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, and the depth-integrated transport in the surface layer, known as Ekman transport, is directed roughly ninety degrees to the right of the wind in deep water. On a shallow shelf where friction dominates, the deflection is smaller, but it is still enough that a wind blowing parallel to a coastline, apparently harmlessly, can drive substantial water toward or away from that coastline. Long stretches of coast oriented along the storm's path can therefore flood without ever experiencing a directly onshore wind. 

This is one of the main reasons surge forecasting cannot be done by intuition. The relationship between what the wind is doing at a location and what the water is doing at that location involves the storm's whole structure, its history over the preceding day, and the shape of the shelf, which is exactly the kind of problem that requires a numerical model rather than a rule of thumb. 

It also explains a pattern that recurs in post-event interviews with survivors. People judge their risk by what they can see and feel, and what they can see and feel is wind. A household on the weak side of a storm may experience frightening gusts and no flooding, conclude that they rode it out successfully, and apply that lesson to the next storm, which passes on the other side and puts three metres of water through the house. Surge risk is a property of location and storm track together, and personal experience of previous storms is among the least reliable guides to it.

sections.heading: Funnels, Bays and Resonance: Local Amplification
sections.body:
The same storm can produce a metre of surge on an open straight coastline and five metres a few tens of kilometres away, and the difference is nearly always geometry. Coastal shape amplifies surge by three related mechanisms, and identifying which apply to a particular stretch of shore is the core of local hazard assessment. 

The first is convergence, sometimes called funnelling. When water driven shoreward enters a bay or embayment that narrows inland, the same volume must fit through a progressively smaller cross-section, and it has nowhere to go but up. The effect is geometric and can be dramatic. Apalachee Bay in Florida's Big Bend, where the coastline forms a right-angled concave corner over a very shallow shelf, is among the most surge-prone stretches in the United States for this reason. The head of the Bay of Bengal is the world's most extreme example, combining convergence with a shallow shelf and a delta whose land surface is often less than three metres above sea level. The Gulf of Mexico funnels of Lake Pontchartrain and the Mississippi River Gulf Outlet channel concentrated Katrina's water against New Orleans in 2005. 

The second is resonance. Any enclosed or semi-enclosed body of water has natural oscillation periods determined by its length and depth, and if a storm's forcing happens to match one of those periods, the response is amplified far beyond the forcing. A long bay open at one end can behave like a quarter-wave resonator, and the sloshing that results, called a seiche, can continue for hours after the wind drops. Great Lakes storms routinely produce seiches of a metre or more, and a shoreline that flooded may flood again as the oscillation returns. 

The third is Proudman resonance, the matching of storm translation speed to the shallow-water wave speed over the shelf. Because that speed is the square root of gravity times depth, a shelf 20 metres deep supports waves at about 14 metres per second, or 50 kilometres per hour, which is squarely within the range of forward speeds that real storms travel. When the match occurs, the disturbance the storm creates travels with the storm and receives energy continuously for hours instead of being left behind. This mechanism explains several documented surges that were much larger than the storm's intensity suggested. 

Rivers add a fourth geometry. A surge propagating up a river channel is confined laterally and can travel far inland, tens of kilometres in some systems, arriving as a rise in water level in towns that consider themselves inland and experience no coastal weather at all. 

Human engineering supplies a fifth. Navigation channels, dredged deep and straight to let ships in, are also excellent conduits for surge, delivering water inland faster and higher than the natural shoreline would. Levees and floodwalls, where they do not enclose an area completely, can channel water along their length and concentrate it at the gap. The lesson from post-event forensic studies is that surge hazard cannot be read off a natural coastline alone; the built waterway network is part of the hydraulic system and sometimes the dominant part.

sections.heading: Tides, Rivers, and Compound Flooding
sections.body:
Surge does not arrive onto a static sea. It arrives onto a tide, and the phase relationship between the two is often the difference between a nuisance and a catastrophe. On a coast with a tidal range of four metres, a surge peaking at low water may leave the total level below the ordinary high-tide mark and flood nothing, while the same surge peaking at high spring tide floods everything. This is not a small correction; on macrotidal coasts such as the Bay of Fundy, the Severn Estuary or parts of northern France, the tide is by far the larger of the two terms. 

The interaction is also nonlinear, which is a genuine complication rather than a technicality. Because wind setup depends inversely on water depth, a surge riding on high tide sits over deeper water and is therefore slightly suppressed relative to the same forcing at low tide, while the friction that slows tidal propagation changes when a surge is present. Total water level is consequently not simply the arithmetic sum of the predicted tide and the modelled surge, and modern forecast systems compute the two together rather than adding them afterward. The residual differences are usually tens of centimetres, occasionally more in shallow estuaries. 

Timing matters at longer periods too. Spring tides, when sun and moon align at new and full moon, produce ranges typically twenty per cent greater than average; perigean spring tides, when the moon is also near its closest approach, add more again. A storm arriving on a perigean spring tide is drawing an unlucky card that is entirely predictable decades in advance, and evacuation planners check it. 

The third water source is fresh. The same storm that pushes seawater inland usually drops enormous rainfall on the catchments draining to that coast, and it does so over hours to days. When high river discharge coincides with high coastal water level, the river cannot discharge because the sea is holding its outlet up, so water backs up behind its own mouth. This is compound flooding, and it is now recognised as a distinct and under-forecast hazard because traditional practice modelled coastal and riverine flooding in separate agencies with separate models. Hurricane Harvey in 2017 and Hurricane Florence in 2018 both produced their worst flooding through this mechanism rather than through surge alone. 

A fourth contributor, easy to overlook, is that heavy rain falling directly onto an area already inundated has nowhere to drain, and pumped drainage systems designed for ordinary storms fail when their outfalls are submerged or their pumps lose power. Urban surge flooding is very often deeper than the surge itself because the drainage network has been disabled from the seaward end.

sections.heading: Waves on Top: Setup, Runup and Overtopping
sections.body:
The surge raises the still-water level. On top of that raised level, waves keep arriving, and for many structures the waves rather than the water level are what actually destroys them. Building a complete picture of coastal flooding therefore requires adding three quantities: the still-water level, which is tide plus surge; the wave setup, which is the additional mean elevation inside the surf zone caused by breaking; and the swash runup, the instantaneous vertical excursion of individual waves rushing up the slope. Together these are called the total water level. 

Wave setup arises because a breaking wave transfers its shoreward momentum to the water column. As waves break across a surf zone, the momentum flux, technically the radiation stress, decreases, and the difference has to be balanced by a tilt in the mean water surface. On a dissipative sandy beach, wave setup at the shoreline is commonly around fifteen to twenty per cent of the offshore significant wave height, so a five-metre offshore sea contributes something like three-quarters of a metre of extra mean elevation before any individual wave is considered. 

Runup depends strongly on how steep the shore is, and the controlling dimensionless quantity is the Iribarren number, the beach slope divided by the square root of the wave steepness. On a gently sloping dissipative beach, waves break far offshore, lose most of their energy in a wide surf zone, and produce relatively modest runup. On a steep reflective beach or a seawall, waves break at or on the structure and can run up several times the offshore wave height. The widely used empirical formula of Stockdon and colleagues, published in 2006, predicts the level exceeded by two per cent of runup events from the offshore wave height, wavelength and beach slope, and remains the standard first estimate. 

Overtopping is the operational concern for defended coasts, and it is measured not as a height but as a mean discharge, litres per second per metre of crest. The distinction matters because a wall is not either overtopped or not; it is overtopped at a rate. European guidance developed through the EurOtop manuals gives approximate tolerance thresholds: pedestrians on a promenade are endangered by mean discharges on the order of a tenth of a litre per second per metre because individual overtopping events are far larger than the mean; vehicles are at risk in the range of a few litres per second per metre; and grass-covered embankments begin to erode somewhere between roughly one and ten litres per second per metre depending on turf quality and how long the loading lasts. These are approximate and depend heavily on structure geometry. 

The practical consequence is that a seawall whose crest stands above the predicted still-water level is not necessarily safe, and that on steep coasts with deep water offshore the entire hazard can be wave-driven even when the surge itself is a few tens of centimetres.

sections.heading: Extratropical Surges and the North Sea Model
sections.body:
Hurricanes and typhoons get the attention, but some of the deadliest surges in recorded history were generated by ordinary mid-latitude depressions, and the physics differs enough that the two cases must be understood separately. 

An extratropical cyclone is much larger than a tropical one, often more than a thousand kilometres across, and moves more slowly relative to its size. Its peak winds are lower, perhaps 100 to 140 kilometres per hour rather than 200, but they blow over an enormous fetch for a day or more rather than for a few hours. Since wind setup integrates stress over distance and time, a broad slow system over a shallow sea can build a surge comparable to a hurricane's. The other key difference is duration: an extratropical surge often persists across two or three successive high tides, so the coast gets repeated chances to be unlucky with tidal phase, and defences that survive one high water may fail on the next. 

The southern North Sea is the archetype, combining every amplifying factor. It is shallow, it narrows southward into the Strait of Dover so that water driven south has nowhere to escape, and the coasts of the Netherlands, Belgium, eastern England and northern Germany are low, densely populated and heavily reclaimed. On the night of 31 January 1953 a deep depression tracked around northern Scotland and into the North Sea, generating northwesterly gales that drove water into the funnel at the same time as a high spring tide. Levels exceeded normal by more than three metres in places. Dikes in the Dutch province of Zeeland, degraded by wartime neglect, failed in hundreds of places. About 1,836 people died in the Netherlands, 307 in England and 28 in Belgium, with hundreds more lost at sea. 

The response defined modern coastal engineering. The Netherlands built the Delta Works, a programme of dams, sluices and storm surge barriers spanning decades, including the Oosterschelde barrier completed in 1986 and the Maeslant barrier protecting Rotterdam completed in 1997, and raised its statutory protection standards to return periods measured in thousands of years for the most populous areas. Britain built the Thames Barrier, operational from 1982. Hamburg, after its own catastrophic flood in 1962 killed over three hundred people, rebuilt its defences comprehensively. 

The results are measurable. When Cyclone Xaver drove North Sea levels in December 2013 to heights comparable with 1953 in some locations, the death toll across the affected countries was a tiny fraction of the earlier disaster. Warning systems and engineering, applied consistently over sixty years, converted a mass-casualty event into a disruption. 

The same physics operates on other mid-latitude coasts with less famous defences. Nor'easters on the eastern seaboard of North America generate surges of one to two metres that, arriving on spring tides and persisting through several tidal cycles, cause severe beach erosion and repeated inundation; the Ash Wednesday storm of March 1962 flooded the mid-Atlantic coast over five successive high tides. The Baltic, the Sea of Azov and the Gulf of Riga all produce extratropical surges, and the barrier protecting Saint Petersburg, completed in 2011, exists for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: Meteotsunamis: The Surge That Is Not a Surge
sections.body:
A distinct and frequently misidentified phenomenon deserves separate treatment, because it looks like a small tsunami, is generated by weather, and catches people out precisely because it does not fit either category cleanly. A meteotsunami is a wave in the tsunami frequency band, with a period between roughly two minutes and two hours, generated not by an earthquake but by a rapidly moving atmospheric disturbance. 

The mechanism is a chain of resonances. A squall line, derecho or fast-moving pressure jump crosses the sea surface. The pressure change is small, typically only one to six hectopascals, which by the inverse barometer effect alone would lift the sea by a few centimetres. But if the disturbance travels at close to the shallow-water wave speed over the shelf, the ocean's response travels with it and is continuously reinforced, the Proudman resonance mechanism again. That amplified long wave then enters a bay or harbour whose natural oscillation period matches its own, and harbour resonance amplifies it further. A few centimetres of atmospheric forcing becomes a wave of one to several metres. 

The phenomenon is well known regionally and carries local names that predate the physics. In Ciutadella harbour on Menorca it is the rissaga, which routinely produces oscillations over a metre and has exceeded four metres, wrecking moored boats. In Nagasaki Bay it is the abiki, which reached about 4.8 metres in 1979. Sicily has the marrobbio and the Croatian Adriatic the šćiga. The Great Lakes produce them too; a wave on Lake Michigan in June 1954 swept fishermen off a Chicago breakwater and killed seven people. On 13 June 2013 a derecho crossing the United States East Coast generated a meteotsunami recorded on gauges from New Jersey to Florida, and three people were swept off a breakwater at Barnegat Inlet. 

The danger is entirely in the surprise. A meteotsunami frequently arrives after the squall has passed and the weather looks improved, from a sea that appears calm, with no earthquake to trigger any warning system. It manifests as a rapid rise and fall repeating every few minutes to tens of minutes, often accompanied by violent currents in harbour mouths and inlets, which is what drowns swimmers and capsizes small boats even when the amplitude is modest. 

Detection and warning remain immature compared with seismic tsunami warning. Some meteorological services now issue advisories when the atmospheric conditions favour them, but the lead times are short and the false alarm problem is severe. The practical guidance is behavioural: after a fast-moving squall line crosses a coast, stay off breakwaters, jetties and low piers, and treat unusual repeated water level oscillations as a reason to leave the water's edge.

sections.heading: Measuring and Forecasting Surge
sections.body:
Surge is measured by tide gauges, permanent installations that record water level continuously against a fixed vertical datum, and the surge itself is extracted by subtracting the astronomically predicted tide from the observation. The resulting residual is the storm surge. Gauge networks are dense in wealthy countries and sparse elsewhere, and gauges have a habit of failing during exactly the events they exist to measure, either because power and telemetry are lost or because the water rises above the sensor. This is why agencies deploy temporary pressure sensors along a forecast track before landfall and why post-event high-water-mark surveys, in which teams record debris lines and mud stains on buildings and survey their elevations, remain essential. 

Forecasting is done with numerical hydrodynamic models solving the shallow-water equations on a grid of the coast and shelf, forced by a modelled wind and pressure field. The United States National Weather Service runs SLOSH, a fast model with basin-specific grids designed to be run thousands of times, whose accuracy is generally quoted as roughly plus or minus twenty per cent of peak surge given perfect meteorological input. Higher-resolution unstructured-grid models such as ADCIRC, Delft3D, SCHISM and FVCOM resolve individual channels and levees and are typically coupled to a wave model like SWAN so that wave setup is included consistently. 

The dominant source of forecast error is not the hydrodynamics. It is the storm. A modest error in forecast track shifts the location of the right-front quadrant, which can move the surge maximum tens of kilometres and change the water level at a given town by metres. Since average track errors at 48 hours are still on the order of one hundred kilometres, a deterministic surge forecast issued two days out is close to meaningless as a point prediction. 

The response is probabilistic. Systems such as the United States P-Surge run the hydrodynamic model hundreds of times with track, intensity and size perturbed according to the historical distribution of forecast errors, and report the result as an exceedance probability: the water level that has, say, a ten per cent chance of being exceeded. Separately, for planning rather than real time, models are run for thousands of hypothetical storms to produce a Maximum Envelope of Water for each category and direction, and the maximum of those envelopes defines evacuation zones. 

One recurring practical trap is vertical datums. A gauge may report relative to mean lower low water, a survey to a national geodetic datum, and a resident's mental model to the height of their own floor. Confusing these produces errors of a metre or more in either direction, which is the whole margin between safety and drowning.

sections.heading: Maps, Warnings, and the Communication Problem
sections.body:
Getting the physics right is only half the problem. Surge warnings have historically failed not because forecasts were wrong but because people did not act on them, and a substantial research literature now exists on why. 

The first failure was the category number. For decades the Saffir-Simpson scale published surge ranges alongside wind speeds, and people reasonably inferred that a category one storm brought a category one surge. Because surge depends far more on size, shelf and geometry than on peak wind, this was wrong often enough to kill people, and the surge ranges were removed in 2010. 

The second was the forecast cone. The cone drawn around a hurricane's projected path shows where the centre of the storm is likely to go, with about a two-thirds probability, and says nothing whatever about where impacts will occur. Impacts routinely extend hundreds of kilometres outside it, and surge in particular can be worst well to the side of the track. People outside the cone have concluded they were not at risk. 

The third was the map datum, discussed as a technical problem but experienced as a communication one. A forecast of three metres of water means nothing to a resident unless it is expressed relative to where they are standing. The United States National Hurricane Center addressed this with the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map, experimental from 2014 and operational from 2016, which shades areas by how deep the water would be above ground level in a reasonable worst case, and with formal Storm Surge Watch and Warning products introduced in 2017 that are issued independently of hurricane wind watches and warnings. The separation matters: a storm can be below hurricane strength and still warrant a life-threatening surge warning. 

A fourth and stubborn problem is that flood insurance maps are not evacuation maps. Insurance mapping is built around a one-per-cent annual chance flood level for rating purposes and is often outdated; evacuation zoning is built around a worst-case surge envelope. A house outside the mapped insurance flood zone can be well inside a surge evacuation zone, and homeowners have refused to leave on the strength of the wrong map. 

The behavioural literature adds a final point that emergency managers now design around. People do not evacuate in response to a number; they evacuate in response to a specific, personalised, credible instruction that names their street or zone, tells them where to go, and is repeated by multiple trusted sources. Vague regional warnings produce very low compliance. Naming the zone, stating the expected depth in metres above the ground, and stating the deadline produce substantially better ones. Concrete framings outperform abstract ones by a wide margin: telling a household that water will reach the first-floor ceiling of a single-storey house moves more people than any probability.

sections.heading: What the Water Actually Does to People and Buildings
sections.body:
Surge kills mainly by drowning, but the mechanics of how people end up in the water are worth spelling out because they are counter-intuitive and because the thresholds are lower than almost anyone expects. 

Moving water destabilises a standing adult at a combination of depth and speed usually expressed as their product. Around half a square metre per second, which is roughly half a metre of water moving at one metre per second, is enough to sweep a fit adult off their feet, and the threshold for children and elderly people is far lower. In practice about fifteen centimetres of fast-moving water is enough. Vehicles are worse, not better: a typical car begins to float in around thirty centimetres because it is a sealed buoyant box, and sixty centimetres of moving water will carry away most vehicles including large trucks. A very large share of flood deaths worldwide occur in cars, driven voluntarily into water that looked shallow. 

Structural damage comes from four mechanisms acting at once. Hydrostatic pressure rises linearly with depth, and the total force on a wall rises with the square of it: two metres of water against a wall exerts roughly twenty kilonewtons per metre of length, about two tonnes-force per metre, which is enough to collapse ordinary masonry that was never designed for lateral load. Buoyant uplift acts on anything sealed, at roughly one tonne-force per square metre for each metre of submergence, which floats slabs, tanks, propane cylinders and lightly-built houses off their foundations. Dynamic wave impact adds short, violent loads several times the hydrostatic value. And scour removes the ground itself, with erosion of one to three metres around pile foundations documented routinely, so a structure can fail because its footing is no longer in contact with anything. 

Debris turns the water into a machine. Floating cars, boats, shipping containers, timber and whole building sections become battering rams travelling at the speed of the current, and much of the destruction attributed to water is actually impact. 

The dangers do not end when the water peaks. Floodwater is contaminated with sewage, fuel and chemicals, and warm brackish water carries organisms including Vibrio species that cause rapidly progressing wound infections. Submerged electrical services electrocute. People trapped in attics have drowned within sealed roof spaces, which is why the standing advice is never to enter an attic without a means of cutting through to the roof. In the days after, carbon monoxide poisoning from generators and cooking equipment run indoors is consistently one of the largest single causes of post-storm death. 

Hypothermia is the quiet one. Water conducts heat from the body roughly twenty-five times faster than air, so a person immersed for hours in water at twenty-five degrees Celsius, which feels warm to the hand, will cool steadily and lose the coordination needed to hold onto anything or climb. In surge events in temperate latitudes, exhaustion and cold rather than an initial submersion are frequently what finally drowns people who survived the first hour.

sections.heading: Defences: Hard Engineering, Soft Engineering and Where Each Fails
sections.body:
Coastal defence divides into structures that hold water out and landscapes that take energy out, and mature practice uses both, because each fails in ways the other does not. 

Hard defences include earth embankments, concrete floodwalls, seawalls, revetments and movable storm surge barriers. Their strength is that they provide a defined level of protection reliably up to their design condition. Their weakness is the shape of the failure curve: performance is near-perfect right up to the design level and then collapses. An earth levee overtopped by a few centimetres begins eroding on its landward face and can breach within hours, at which point the flood behind it is deeper and faster than if there had been no levee at all, because the water arrives suddenly into a basin. Failures also occur below the design level through seepage and internal erosion, called piping, and through foundation instability. The New Orleans floodwall failures during Katrina in 2005 included sections that gave way before being overtopped, through mechanisms design practice had not anticipated. 

Movable barriers are the most sophisticated form: the Thames Barrier, the Dutch Maeslant and Oosterschelde barriers, the Venice MOSE gates first used successfully in 2020, and the barrier across New Orleans's inner harbour. They leave estuaries open for navigation and close only when needed, at the cost of enormous capital expense and a dependence on correct, timely operational decisions. 

Soft defences work by dissipating energy across a wide, rough, shallow zone. Dunes are extremely effective while they remain intact and offer nothing once breached, which was visible in the sharply different outcomes along adjacent stretches of the New Jersey shore during Sandy in 2012. Coastal wetlands and mangroves attenuate waves strongly; reviews of field measurements find significant wave height reduced by something like thirteen to sixty-six per cent per hundred metres of mangrove, depending on density and species. Their effect on the surge water level itself is real but much more variable, with published estimates ranging from a few centimetres to several tens of centimetres per kilometre of forest, and the honest position is that this range is wide and site-specific rather than a reliable design figure. Coral reefs are the most effective natural structure known, dissipating around ninety-seven per cent of wave energy. 

The most persistent systemic failure is not engineering but behavioural, and it has a name: the levee effect. Building protection encourages development behind it, so when the design condition is eventually exceeded, the consequences are larger than they would have been with no defence at all. 

The third strategy, applied at the scale of the individual building, is neither to exclude the water nor to slow it but to get out of its way vertically. Elevating a house on piles above the design flood level plus a margin of freeboard, with breakaway panels below so that the enclosed space fails harmlessly rather than transmitting load to the frame, is the standard approach on exposed coasts and it works. Where elevation is impractical, managed retreat and voluntary buyout of the most exposed properties is the only measure that reduces risk permanently rather than deferring it.

sections.heading: Sea-Level Rise and the Shifting Baseline
sections.body:
Everything above describes surge relative to the sea level of the day. That baseline is moving, and because extreme water levels have a steeply decaying statistical tail, a modest shift in the baseline produces a disproportionate change in how often any given flood level is reached. 

Global mean sea level has risen roughly twenty to twenty-five centimetres since 1900, and the satellite altimetry record shows the rate accelerating, from under two millimetres a year through much of the twentieth century to around four and a half millimetres a year over the past decade. The two contributions are thermal expansion of warming seawater and added mass from melting land ice, with the ice contribution growing as a share. 

The statistical amplification is the part that matters operationally and is widely misunderstood. Because the distribution of annual maximum water levels falls off roughly exponentially in its upper tail, adding a fixed offset to every event multiplies the exceedance frequency rather than adding to it. In many locations, ten centimetres of sea-level rise roughly doubles how often a given threshold is crossed, and studies have projected that in numerous tropical and subtropical coastal cities the level currently exceeded once a century will be exceeded annually within decades. This is why sunny-day flooding, streets going under at high tide with no storm at all, has become routine in places where it was rare a generation ago; it is the leading edge of the same shift. 

What actually matters at any given town is relative sea level, which combines the global signal with vertical land motion. Land subsidence, driven by sediment compaction, groundwater and hydrocarbon extraction and post-glacial adjustment, can dwarf the global rate. Parts of coastal Louisiana are sinking at close to a centimetre a year. Jakarta has subsided by metres in some districts because of groundwater pumping, at rates far above any climate signal, which is a central reason Indonesia decided to relocate its capital. Semarang, Manila, Bangkok and Ho Chi Minh City face versions of the same problem. 

Whether storms themselves are becoming more surge-productive is a separate and more contested question. There is reasonable evidence that the proportion of tropical cyclones reaching the highest intensities has increased and that rainfall rates have risen with atmospheric moisture. Claims about changes in storm size, forward speed and poleward migration are actively debated and the observational records are short. The rising baseline, by contrast, is not in doubt, and on the timescale of most coastal infrastructure it is the dominant term. 

The practical implication for anyone assessing a specific property is that historical flood experience is a decaying guide. A house that has flooded twice in fifty years has not established a once-in-twenty-five-year risk that will persist; it has established a rate under a sea level that no longer exists. Design and purchase decisions with a fifty-year horizon should be made against the projected water level at the end of that horizon, plus a margin, not against the record. Where the land is also subsiding, that projection must use relative rather than global sea-level figures, which for some deltas doubles or triples the number.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and What To Do When the Water Comes
sections.body:
The failure modes that kill people in surge events are remarkably consistent across countries and decades. The first is judging risk by wind category, which as established has little relationship to surge. The second is judging risk by personal history, when the previous storm passed on the favourable side. The third is late departure: roads flood and bridges close well before the storm arrives, and emergency services suspend rescue once sustained winds pass roughly sixty-five kilometres per hour, so a household that waits for conditions to look serious has already missed the window. The fourth is driving into water. The fifth is sheltering in a single-storey coastal building. The sixth is returning too early, into water that is contaminated, electrified and hiding scoured-out road surfaces. 

What follows is the standard sequence used by coastal emergency management, condensed. It assumes you have official warnings; if you do not, the physical cues are a falling barometer, a rising and unusually long-period swell, and water already higher than the tide table says it should be.
steps: Before any storm is forecast, find out two numbers: which surge evacuation zone your address is in, and how many metres above the tidal datum your ground floor sits. Write them down. Almost nobody knows the second number and it is the one that decides everything.

When a storm surge watch is issued, typically about 48 hours ahead, treat it as the decision point rather than the warning. Fuel the vehicle, draw cash, refill prescriptions, charge everything, photograph documents, and identify a specific destination and a specific departure time.

When a surge warning or an evacuation order is issued, roughly 36 hours ahead, leave. Do not wait for the order to be upgraded and do not wait for visible weather. Departure must be complete before sustained winds reach about 65 kilometres per hour.

Go inland or uphill, not far away. Tens of kilometres inland or a few tens of metres of elevation is enough to escape surge entirely, and a short evacuation is far more likely to be completed than a long one that puts you on a gridlocked motorway when the wind arrives.

Never drive through moving water of unknown depth. Thirty centimetres floats a car; the road underneath may have been scoured away entirely. Turn around and take another route, including if it costs hours.

If you are trapped and the water is rising, move upward, but take tools capable of cutting through a roof and do not enter a sealed attic without them. Carry a charged phone in a sealed bag, a whistle and a light. Mark your position visibly from above if you can.

After the water drops, wait for an official all-clear. Assume every downed line is live, do not run a generator or any combustion appliance indoors or in a garage, and treat any wound exposed to floodwater as needing prompt medical review.

guides.safetyNote: Storm surge is the leading killer in most coastal storms and it drowns people who stayed because the wind forecast sounded survivable. Evacuate on the water forecast, not the wind category, and leave before winds reach about 65 km/h, when bridges close and rescue stops. Never drive into moving water: 30 cm floats most cars and 15 cm of fast water will knock an adult down. If you are trapped, go up but never into a sealed attic without a way onto the roof.

guides.title: Levee Breach Behavior and Warning Time
guides.summary: How levees fail, how a breach grows and floods the land behind it, why warning time is so short, and what monitoring, flood fighting, planning, and immediate personal action can do about it.

sections.heading: Why a Levee Breach Is Not an Ordinary Flood
sections.body: A levee is an embankment, usually of compacted earth, built along a river, canal, or coastline to keep high water off the land behind it. Unlike a dam, which blocks a valley and holds a permanent reservoir, a levee normally stands dry and is loaded only during floods, sometimes for a few hours in a storm surge, sometimes for months in a great river flood. That difference in duty produces a difference in danger. When a river without levees rises, the flood arrives gradually: water creeps up over days, forecasts track it, and people can usually move themselves and their property in time. When a levee breaches, the flood arrives as a catastrophe in miniature: a wall of water pours through a gap that may grow to hundreds of meters wide, moving at several meters per second near the opening, and land that was dry an hour earlier can lie under two, three, or four meters of water by nightfall. The protected area behind a levee is very often lower than the flood itself, sometimes lower than the normal river, because levee-building encourages settlement of low ground and because drained soils subside over decades; parts of New Orleans, the Sacramento delta, and the Dutch polders lie below the water they hold back every single day. That geometry means breach flooding does not politely stop; it keeps pouring until the river drops, the gap is closed, or the basin behind fills to the brim. Compounding the physics is a well-documented human pattern that hazard researchers call the levee effect: protection encourages development, development raises the stakes, and decades without a flood breed the belief that the flood cannot come. The result, repeated on every continent, is that levee breaches kill people who did not think they lived in a floodplain and destroy property whose owners carried no flood insurance. The warning problem is the heart of the matter and the reason this guide pairs breach behavior with warning time. River crests can be forecast days ahead, but the failure of a particular kilometer of levee generally cannot; a levee can stand all day against a flood and fail in the last hour of the crest, or fail below its design level through a hidden defect, as happened catastrophically in New Orleans in 2005. Warnings for breach floods are therefore conditional, late, or absent, and the people nearest the breach may have only minutes. Understanding how breaches actually develop, what the water does once it is through, and how the warning chain works, and fails, is the practical foundation for living safely behind these structures, and that understanding begins with the anatomy of the embankment itself.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Levee and the Load a Flood Applies
sections.body: A typical earthen levee is a long trapezoidal prism. Its top surface, the crest or crown, commonly carries a patrol road; the waterside slope faces the river and the landside slope faces the protected area, each usually pitched between one vertical on two horizontal and one on four or flatter. The vertical margin between the design flood level and the crest is the freeboard, often around one meter, and it is the levee's first reserve against surprise. Good levees are built of compacted soil in layers called lifts, ideally with a core of low-permeability clay to resist water passing through and shells of stronger material for stability; many real levees, especially old agricultural ones, are instead whatever soil was at hand, dumped and shaped by generations of repair, and their internal composition is genuinely unknown even to their owners. The levee sits on a foundation of natural floodplain deposits, and this matters enormously: floodplains are layered sandwiches of sands, silts, clays, and buried organic soils marking old channels and swamps, and water and weakness travel through the foundation as readily as through the embankment. Ancillary features complete the system: berms that widen the base to lengthen seepage paths, riprap or revetment armoring the waterside against current and waves, toe drains and relief wells on the landside that give seeping water a safe controlled exit, floodwalls of concrete where space is tight, and gates, ramps, and pipe crossings wherever human traffic and utilities must pass through the line. When a flood arrives, it applies three loads at once. The first is hydrostatic pressure, proportional to the depth of water against the slope, pushing the structure landward. The second is seepage: water enters the soil and moves through both embankment and foundation toward the lower landside, and as the flood persists, the saturated zone inside the levee, whose upper boundary engineers call the phreatic surface, migrates downstream through the embankment. Saturation is corrosive to stability in two ways: it adds weight while destroying the suction that helps unsaturated soil hold together, and it raises pore water pressure, which carries part of the load between soil grains and thereby reduces the friction that gives soil its strength. The third load is attack at the surface: current scouring the waterside toe, wind waves pounding and running up the slope, debris battering, and rain softening the crest. Duration is the silent multiplier of all three. A levee that shrugs off a two-day crest may fail on the tenth day of the same water level simply because seepage has had time to saturate and pressurize it; the great Mississippi flood of 1993 held levees under load for weeks and failed hundreds of them. Every failure mode that follows is one of these loads finding a weakness faster than the levee can drain, resist, or be defended.

sections.heading: Overtopping: The Most Visible Road to Failure
sections.body: Overtopping is the failure mode everyone can picture: the water rises higher than the levee, spills over the crest, and the falling sheet of water attacks the landside slope. It is the dominant cause of levee failure worldwide, responsible by most tallies for something like two-thirds of breaches, and it is also the mode most nearly forecastable, since it requires the river or surge to exceed a known crest elevation. What is less widely understood is that overtopping does not breach a levee instantly; it breaches by erosion, and the race between erosion and flood duration decides the outcome. When water first tops the crest, it flows as a thin fast sheet down the landside slope, and the slope's covering decides how long it survives. A dense, well-rooted grass cover on cohesive soil can withstand shallow overtopping, on the order of a few tens of centimeters, for hours before it fails; bare sand may begin unraveling in minutes. Erosion almost never starts uniformly. It seizes on irregularities, a rut, an animal path, a fence post, a patch of thin grass, and concentrates flow there, cutting rills that merge into a channel. The critical development is the headcut: a small vertical step in the slope where falling water undermines the soil, and which then migrates uphill, upstream against the flow, eating toward the crest like a moving waterfall. When the headcut slices through the crest, the game changes abruptly, because now the effective top of the levee is lower at that point, more water pours through the notch, the extra flow erodes faster, and a feedback loop begins that turns a wet crossing into a growing breach. From first overtopping to full breach can take anywhere from under an hour on a sandy levee under deep overflow to many hours on well-built clay under a skim of water, which is why flood fighters sandbag crests and lay plastic sheeting on slopes: buying hours is often buying survival, since river crests pass. Wave overtopping, the coastal and lake variant, is nastier per unit of water because waves arrive as repeated slugs and impacts rather than a steady sheet, hammering the crest and rear slope; the North Sea storm of 1953 destroyed Dutch and English defenses largely through wave attack on rear slopes that were never armored, a lesson that rebuilt coastal engineering in both countries. Deliberate, engineered overtopping is also a tool: spillway sections and fuse-plug levees are built lower or weaker on purpose so that an extreme flood relieves itself over a chosen, armored stretch of farmland instead of bursting through an unchosen one, the principle behind the floodways on the Mississippi, and the intentional crevassing of the Birds Point floodway in 2011. For anyone watching a levee in a flood, the operational signs are simple: water at or over the crest anywhere, or a visible notch or waterfall on the landside slope, means breach formation may already be underway, and the time for evacuation is immediately.

sections.heading: Internal Erosion and Piping: The Hidden Killer
sections.body: The most treacherous levee failures happen with the river still below the crest, sometimes well below it, when the levee is defeated not over its top but through its body or its foundation. Engineers group these mechanisms as internal erosion, and the classic form is called piping. The physics begins with seepage. Water standing high against a levee pushes through the pores of the soil toward the lower landside, and the strength of that push at any point is measured by the hydraulic gradient, the drop in water pressure per unit distance of travel. Where seeping water exits the ground on the landside, it exerts an upward drag on soil grains, and if the exit gradient approaches a critical value, roughly one for typical sands, meaning a pressure head falling about a meter per meter of path, the drag cancels the grains' buoyant weight and the sand liquefies into a boiling, mobile state. Grains begin to wash out at the exit, and their removal shortens the seepage path, which steepens the gradient, which accelerates the washing: a self-enlarging tunnel, the pipe, erodes backward from the exit point toward the river. If it connects, the river gains a direct pressurized conduit under or through the levee; flow roars through, the tunnel enlarges, its roof collapses, and the levee slumps into a breach, often with little external warning until the final minutes. Piping caused roughly a third of historical levee failures and some of the deadliest, precisely because it ignores freeboard: a levee with a meter of dry margin can be dissolving underneath. Several variants matter. Backward erosion piping proper favors clean fine sands in the foundation, typically where a thin natural blanket of clay on the landside confines a sandy substratum; pressure beneath the blanket can also heave it bodily upward, cracking it and opening exits. Concentrated leak erosion follows a pre-existing defect, a desiccation crack, a poorly compacted lift, the loosened annulus around a pipe or culvert through the levee, an old tree root hole, and erodes its walls.
